transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-17
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 mins
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Samir Shah (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Redwood CSM); Emily Carter (RiverMark Eng Lead), Ravi Singh (RiverMark SRE), Tina Lopez (RiverMark PM)

Summary:
Quick sync on POC latency numbers, focused on TTFT (time-to-first-token), streaming behaviour, sequence length distribution impact, and kernel selection tradeoffs. Agreed to run a 2k token TTFT benchmark on dedicated pool and share profiler logs; RiverMark to provide sequence histograms. Discussed fallback streaming vs non-streamed batching for UI flows; small discrepancies in profiler naming (nvprof vs our runtime traces) noted.

Topics:
- TTFT benchmarks and anomalies
- Streaming vs non-streaming latency tradeoffs
- Sequence length distribution and batching effects
- Kernel choices and quantization profile impact
- Next steps and ownership

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Kim: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um we have about 45 minutes, agenda is TTFT and streaming follow-up from last week
[00:12] Emily Carter: yeah thanks Jordan, we ran the quick test you sent over, we saw a big variance on TTFT when the sequence prefix is long, i think up to 300ms spike sometimes
[00:23] Samir Shah: yeah that's consistent with what we expected, when prefix is large the KV cache fill and attention kernel selection can cause first-token to jump, sometimes we pick a slower kernel path for long context, uh we want to check kernel selection logs
[00:40] Ravi Singh: quick question, are you guys running dynamic kernel switching in the dedicated pool or is that something in the hosted path?
[00:48] Samir Shah: good question, in dedicated we enable our runtime to select kernels based on sequence length heuristics, but there are edge conditions where it falls back to a more conservative kernel, which increases TTFT, that's what we're seeing
[01:02] Tina Lopez: from product side the UX cares about TTFT for the first message in a chat, streaming helps but users often judge the perceived latency by time-to-first-token
[01:14] Jordan Kim: exactly, so two levers: streaming to start emitting partial tokens earlier and kernel/config tuning to reduce setup cost. we recommended q4h quant profile earlier to save throughput cost, but q4h vs q8 has different kernel code paths, did that come up in your tests?
[01:33] Emily Carter: we tried q4h and the cost was good but TTFT seemed slightly worse, maybe the dequant step adds overhead? also our prompts have fairly long template text, like ~600 tokens prefix for some flows
[01:45] Samir Shah: right, dequant and layout changes can add a few ms, but usually the bigger hit is memory layout and kernel launch overhead for unusual seq lengths. if you can share your prefix histograms we can simulate more accurately
[02:02] Emily Carter: yes i'll upload a CSV to the shared drive after the call
[02:07] Samir Shah: awesome, and we'll run a controlled TTFT bench with 2k sample points across your seq distribution, and dump the kernel selection trace, nvprof, and our runtime event logs
[02:18] Ravi Singh: what's your hypothesis on streaming vs non-streamed for our web UI? currently we do non-streamed to get a single response and post-process on client
[02:28] Jordan Kim: non-streamed simplifies client but increases perceived wait; streaming gives earlier partials but requires client handling. also streaming impacts throughput and scheduling slightly since we hold open the connection and can affect batch timing
[02:41] Tina Lopez: we can do streaming on the web client, but we need guidance on how to balance small prefix responses vs cost. users expect first word under 400ms ideally
[02:52] Samir Shah: for that SLO we should tune to reduce TTFT by prioritizing first-token paths: pre-warm KV cache for common prefixes, use a streaming-first kernel where possible, and adjust batch window to allow immediate flush for small requests
[03:08] Emily Carter: about pre-warm, is that manual or automatic? we have a set of templated prompts across 10k daily users but only a few hundred distinct templates
[03:17] Samir Shah: we have prefix caching options, automatic prefix caching for hot prefixes can be enabled — tradeoff is memory usage in the accelerator and cache eviction policy, we can propose a config for your distribution
[03:29] Jordan Kim: also wanted to call out that our runtime has a small startup jitter when a kernel path hasn't been JIT'd yet on the machine, so when you move to a fresh instance you'll sometimes see a 50-120ms extra TTFT for the first request. for Dedicated we can keep warm instances pinned to reduce that
[03:48] Ravi Singh: that explains spikes we saw on cold scale-outs. question on profiling: will your profiler require debug symbols or can we run it in our staging with limited permissions?
[03:58] Samir Shah: we can run lightweight runtime traces without elevated privileges; for deeper nvprof traces we might need a staging GPU instance with profiler enabled. we'll give you exact steps and a short script
[04:12] Emily Carter: cool. also we saw an odd thing where streaming tokens arrived but were a bit garbled for certain long sequences, i'm not sure if that's tokenization or streaming truncation
[04:24] Samir Shah: probably tokenization or an off-by-one in our streaming buffer flush; we've seen that when the sequence is near the max and we do an aggressive chunking policy. we'll reproduce in our bench and include the flags we used
[04:38] Tina Lopez: good. can you remind us of the tradeoffs between q4h and q8 in terms of first-token latency and throughput?
[04:47] Samir Shah: in our experience q4h reduces memory and improves throughput for long-run sustained traffic, but q4h dequant step adds a small per-request overhead versus q8 which keeps FP16 path; so q8 tends to have lower TTFT but higher memory/TCO. exact numbers depend on model size and kernels; we'll show numbers for your workload
[05:06] Jordan Kim: i'll add that kernel choice matters: some attention kernels are optimized for short sequences and some for long; the runtime chooses based on sequence length heuristics, but you can pin kernel sets if you prefer deterministic behaviour
[05:21] Emily Carter: pinning might help for predictability, but we care about cost too. can we do A/B: pinned for low-latency VIP users, auto for the rest?
[05:30] Samir Shah: yes, the rollout can do canary/pinned per-route. that's part of the Dedicated config sheet I'll share.
[05:38] Jordan Kim: quick note on metrics: we'll provide token-level breakdowns, TTFT histograms, and per-route latency. those will be visible in Console once we onboard the Dedicated pool
[05:47] Ravi Singh: ok, regarding SLA, if we pin capacity for some routes, does SLA guarantee latency or just availability?
[05:55] Jordan Kim: availability and throughput are in the SLA; for latency we provide latency targets with SRE support and we can add latency SLOs into the contract for pinned capacity. we'll involve contracts and solutions engineering for precise language
[06:08] Tina Lopez: for the bench you mentioned can you share the exact config flags so we can mirror them?
[06:13] Samir Shah: yeah i'll include the bench script, kernel flags, and a sample profiler command. i'll drop them in the shared folder: https://rwd.example.com/benchmarks/rivermark-ttft-20260317 (placeholder link)
[06:26] Emily Carter: perfect. any immediate wins we should try for next week?
[06:30] Samir Shah: immediate: enable streaming-first flush for small requests, set batch window to 10ms for interactive routes, and enable prefix caching for top 100 templates. we'll test and report delta
[06:42] Emily Carter: can you estimate the cost impact of those changes? we're sensitive to per-token cost increases if we reduce batching
[06:49] Jordan Kim: tradeoff: smaller batch window increases per-token cost a bit but improves TTFT. prefix caching increases memory footprint but reduces compute per request. Samir will quantify after the bench runs
[07:02] Ravi Singh: also we might try pre-compute some of the templated outputs for super-high-frequency templates as a cache layer in front of Redwood for microsecond responses
[07:12] Tina Lopez: interesting, but we still need fallback path for dynamic inputs.
[07:18] Samir Shah: yeah that layered approach works: pre-compute for top hits, prefix cache for hot templates, streaming-first for interactive fallbacks
[07:27] Jordan Kim: okay let's walk through the bench plan and deliverables -- Samir?
[07:31] Samir Shah: plan: 1) reproduce TTFT variance using your seq hist CSV, 2) run 2k-sample bench across pinned vs runtime kernel selection and q4h vs q8, 3) collect nvprof and runtime traces, 4) produce short report with median/p95 TTFT, token-per-second throughput, and estimated cost delta. we'll aim to deliver by 2026-03-19
[07:54] Emily Carter: sounds good. any blockers from our side? we need to know what credentials to provide for profiler staging
[07:59] Jordan Kim: we'll send a minimal access checklist; Ravi you'll be our infra contact for that
[08:06] Ravi Singh: noted, i'll look for the checklist and confirm whether we can open the required egress to the profiler host
[08:12] Lena Ortiz: i'll follow up with a calendar invite for the profiling session and include the bench artifacts link
[08:18] Tina Lopez: one question on compliance - if we enable profiler, does that leak any customer PII in traces? we can't send traces to your hosted collector with PII
[08:28] Samir Shah: good point; profiler traces are low-level and shouldn't contain payload text, but for caution we'll mask or run traces inside your VPC/proxy and share only aggregated metrics; we'll document exact fields in the checklist
[08:41] Jordan Kim: ok wrap up, let's recap next steps
[08:45] Jordan Kim: recap: Samir runs 2k TTFT bench and shares logs (due 2026-03-19), Emily uploads seq hist CSV (due 2026-03-18), Jordan sends pricing/config and bench materials (due 2026-03-18), schedule profiling session for week of 2026-03-22. Lena to send invites and links.
[09:05] Emily Carter: thanks team, appreciate quick turnaround
[09:09] Jordan Kim: thanks all, we'll talk next week same time, bye
